1. `kia-ev6-2025-lr-rwd` — EV6 2025 Long Range RWD

4. `chevy-equinoxev-awd-2lt` — Equinox EV 2LT AWD
5. `toyota-rav4prime-awd` — RAV4 Prime AWD (PHEV, 18.1 kWh)

Method:
1. WebSearch + Exa MCP IN PARALLEL.
2. Cross-reference EV-Database.org, fueleconomy.gov, kia.ca, chevrolet.ca, toyota.ca.
3. Confidence: High = 2+ sources agree within ±5%.

Return ONE JSON object (under 500 words):

```json
{
  "<vehicle_id>": {
    "<field>": {
      "new_value": <num>,
      "new_confidence": "High",
      "new_source": {"url": "...", "name": "...", "accessed": "2026-04-24"},
      "evidence": "Source A: X; Source B: Y"
    }
  }
}
```

Omit no-upgrade vehicles.

- New to the 2025 Kia EV6 is a standard 63 kWh and an available 84 kWh battery to improve the driving range. At the bottom of this page are charts that show the charging times and all-electric driving ranges for the 2025 EV6.

When looking at the spec sheet for the 2025 Kia EV6, we see five overall trim levels: Light, Light Long Range, Wind, GT-Line, and GT. The standard battery is now 63 kWh, an upgrade from the standard 58 kWh battery pack of the 2024 EV6 Light RWD. Meanwhile, the larger 84 kWh battery for 2025 replaces the 77.4 kWh unit found in all other 2024 EV6 models, including the Long Range and GT-Line variants.
[...]
Kia said the 2025 EV6 Light Long Range, Wind, and GT-Line with RWD could achieve a manufacturer-estimated 319 miles of all-electric range per full charge with the new 84 kWh battery. For context, the 77.4 kWh battery of the 2024 models provided 310 miles of range in these configurations.
[...]
The 2025 EV6 has a starting MSRP of $44,375. The Light Long Range RWD and Light Long Range AWD start at $47,675 and $51,775, respectively. The GT at the top of the lineup starts at $65,275. Those figures include the $1,475 destination charge.

I managed to eke 340 kilometres out of my all-wheel-drive 2025 EV6 on a single battery charge. That works out to about 25 kilowatt-hours per 100 kilometres. That’s pretty much business as usual from a Kia/Hyundai crossover. Not only is that smack dab in the efficiency range I’ve previously experienced, it was almost exactly what the GT-Line’s efficiency meter was displaying. That might seem like a small point — the honesty, not the efficiency — but considering the lies that some energy efficiency meters tell, it’s much appreciated. That said, that’s it for trustworthiness; the EV6’s range remaining estimator, like so many others, was hopelessly optimistic.
[...]
It’s also worth noting that my tester, thanks to its 20-inch wheels, boasted the shortest range of any of the bigger-batteried EV6s. Opting for some smaller 19-inchers on a dual-motor EV6, for instance, boosts range by a full 40 kilometres says NRCan. As with all things, being a slave to fashion can cost beacoup bucks. One other upgrade worth noting is that, with the bigger battery, comes enhanced towing ability, the 2025 AWD versions of the EV6 now able to haul 2,700 pounds.
[...]
Other, more minor, upgrades include chassis reinforcements to meet the IIHS’s increasingly stringent crash standards, additional sound-deadening materials round the cabin and an upgraded digital key. MSRP for the EV6 is $58,495 and our GT-line would have cost $67,495 (that is sans taxes, but does include $2,195 freight and air conditioning taxes). Considering that the GT-Line package contains such goodies as front and rear heated seats and ventilation for the buckets up front as well as a Meridian sound system and a head-up display, the overall package passes for something of a bargain in EV circles.
